claims.claim_text: Can't Stop's four-dice probabilities and forced-move rule make it nearly balanced, and simulations show probabilistic, consistent play wins, though going first is a large advantage.
claims.evidence_quote: The game heavily favors middle columns.
claims.reasoning: Probabilistic consistency and first-player advantage are supported, but source says combination play is badly imbalanced, not 'nearly balanced'.

claims.claim_text: Can't Stop has players roll four dice, pair them into sums, and advance markers on columns 2 through 12, needing three completed columns to win.
claims.evidence_quote: roll four dice, pair them up however you want, move your markers on a board ... You need to complete three columns to win.
claims.reasoning: Source states the four-dice, pairing, column and three-column win rules directly.

claims.claim_text: You can keep rolling as long as you want, but busting when no marker can move loses the turn's gains.
claims.evidence_quote: you can keep rolling as long as you want, but if you can't move any of your three active markers, you lose everything you've gained that turn.
claims.reasoning: Matches source wording on continued rolling and losing accumulated progress on bust.

claims.claim_text: Column lengths run 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 11, 9, 7, 5, and 3 steps for columns 2 through 12.
claims.evidence_quote: Columns 2 and 12: 3 steps ... Column 7: 13 steps
claims.reasoning: Sequence matches the source's column length list exactly.

claims.claim_text: The forced-move rule requires taking all legal moves from a chosen pairing, even unwanted ones.
claims.evidence_quote: you must take all available moves ... you must make ALL legal moves from that pairing, even if you don't want them.
claims.reasoning: Direct restatement of the forced-move rule.

claims.claim_text: On {6,7,8}, rolling (1,1,3,4) and pairing 2+7 forces moving both 2 and 7 as well.
claims.evidence_quote: you could choose pairing (1,1)+(3,4) = 2+7. But if you do, you're forced to take BOTH the 2 and the 7
claims.reasoning: Source gives exactly this example with the same dice and columns.

claims.claim_text: The forced-move rule prevents trivial play and adds tactical depth.
claims.evidence_quote: This rule prevents the game from being trivially easy and adds tactical depth.
claims.reasoning: Near-verbatim restatement of source conclusion.

claims.claim_text: An interactive web version exists with a Python/FastAPI backend and React frontend.
claims.evidence_quote: I've implemented a fully interactive web version of the game with a Python/FastAPI backend and React frontend.
claims.reasoning: Directly stated in the source.

claims.claim_text: Four dice flatten the distribution: P(7) rises to 64.4% and P(2) to 13.2%, far closer together than with two dice.
claims.evidence_quote: P(7) = 64.4% vs P(2) = 13.2%, only a 4.88× difference compared to 6× with two dice
claims.reasoning: Numbers match the source's four-dice flattening claim.

claims.claim_text: With two dice, sum 7 is most likely at 16.67% and exactly 6× more likely than sum 2 at 2.78%.
claims.evidence_quote: Sum 7 is the most likely at 16.67%, and it's exactly 6× more likely than sum 2 at 2.78%.
claims.reasoning: Exact restatement of source values.

claims.claim_text: Sum 2 requires both dice showing 1 (1/36); sum 7 has 6 order-sensitive ways: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4).
claims.evidence_quote: both dice must show 1. That's 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36 ... complementary pairs: (1,6), (2,5), or (3,4), and order matters, so that's 6 ways
claims.reasoning: Matches the source proof exactly.

claims.claim_text: If Can't Stop used two dice, column 7 would need to be 6× longer than column 2, but it is only 13/3 ≈ 4.3×.
claims.evidence_quote: column 7 would need to be 6× longer than column 2 to be equally hard. Instead it's only 13/3 ≈ 4.3× longer.
claims.reasoning: Values and framing match the source.

claims.claim_text: Rolling 2, 3, 4, 5 gives just three pairings: 5 and 9, 6 and 8, or 7 and 7.
claims.reasoning: Exact list from the source.

claims.claim_text: Four dice give P(can make a 2) = 171/1296 ≈ 13.2%, requiring at least two 1s among the four.
claims.reasoning: Fraction and percentage match the source calculation.
Intermediate probabilities match the source exactly.

claims.claim_text: Four dice give P(can make a 7) = 834/1296 ≈ 64.4%, via inclusion-exclusion over pairs (1,6), (2,5), (3,4).
claims.reasoning: Result and method match the source.

claims.claim_text: Each pair event has probability 302/1296, each pairwise overlap 24/1296, and the triple overlap is 0.
claims.reasoning: All three component values match the source.
Exact arithmetic restatement from source.

claims.claim_text: The full four-dice table shows at-least-one-pair counts from 171 (13.2%) for sum 2 up to 834 (64.4%) for sum 7.
claims.reasoning: Table endpoints match the source table.

claims.claim_text: The probability ratio from column 2 to 7 is 4.88 against a length ratio of 4.33, close enough to suggest deliberate design.
claims.evidence_quote: The probability ratio from 2 to 7 is 4.88. The length ratio is 4.33. Pretty close! The game designers were definitely thinking about this.
claims.reasoning: Ratios and design inference match the source.

claims.claim_text: The conclusion restates this: four-dice probabilities flatten the distribution, with P(7) = 64.4% versus P(2) = 13.2%, only a 4.88× difference.
claims.evidence_quote: Four-dice probabilities flatten the distribution - P(7) = 64.4% vs P(2) = 13.2%, only a 4.88× difference
claims.reasoning: Matches the source conclusion item verbatim.

claims.claim_text: Single columns are nearly balanced: expected rolls stay between 19.60 and 22.73 across all columns.
claims.reasoning: Min and max of the source table match the stated range.

claims.claim_text: Expected rolls equal length over probability: column 2 needs 3/0.132 = 22.73 rolls; column 7 needs 13/0.644 = 20.18.
claims.evidence_quote: For column 2: 3/0.132 = 22.73 rolls, For column 7: 13/0.644 = 20.18 rolls
claims.reasoning: Formula and values match the source.

claims.claim_text: Column 7 is slightly faster than column 2 even though it is 4× longer.
claims.evidence_quote: Column 7 is slightly faster, even though it's 4× longer.
claims.reasoning: Near-verbatim source statement.
All listed values match the source table.

claims.claim_text: Columns 2 and 12 require the most rolls; columns 6, 7, and 8 cluster near 20.
claims.evidence_quote: Columns 2 and 12 require the most rolls. Columns 6, 7, and 8 are all close to each other around 20 rolls.
claims.reasoning: Direct restatement of source observation.

claims.claim_text: Column 2 is only 3 steps but hit 13.2% of the time; column 7 is 13 steps but hit 64.4% of the time.
claims.evidence_quote: column 2 is only 3 steps ... you'll only hit it 13.2% of the time. Column 7 is 13 steps but you hit it 64.4% of the time.
claims.reasoning: Steps and percentages match the source.

fail_list: C01 partially supported: summary labels the game 'nearly balanced', but source states combination play heavily favors middle columns
